Ja'Marr Chase draws a plus matchup — JAX concede 68 yds/game to WR1s (league ~58), and CIN funnel 29% of targets his way. A rec-yards spot.

The CIN host the JAX as favorites of 2.5, with the total set at 51.5 — a market that implies a CIN 27–24 scoreline. Running the game forward from that baseline, we expect a contest that spends roughly 26% of its snaps with CIN in front, 39% within one score, and 34% with CIN chasing. That distribution is the engine of everything below: game state is what turns a team's tendencies into a specific player's workload, so before we get to individuals it's worth being explicit about how this game is likely to be played.

This is a coin-flip script. With only 2.5 points separating them, neither team projects to spend much time in a blowout state — most of the game lives in the 'close' bucket, where play-calling stays balanced and usage tracks each player's established role rather than being distorted by score. In tight games the stars on both sides see their normal, dependable workloads, and there is less garbage-time leakage to backups.

The Key Matchups

CIN are soft against the run (137 yds/game allowed), and JAX feed Chris Rodriguez Jr. a heavy 57% carry share — a rushing-yards spot.

Tough sledding for Chase Brown — JAX are stingy against the run (109 yds/game, well below the ~120 norm); lean under on his rushing line.

Joe Burrow has a passing-yards tailwind — JAX allow 252 pass yds/game (vs ~230).

Trevor Lawrence has a passing-yards tailwind — CIN allow 241 pass yds/game (vs ~230).

Brenton Strange has room to work — CIN allow 46 yds/game to TE1s (vs ~35), a receiving-yards and target angle.

Sneaky value on Tee Higgins (WR2) — JAX leak 44 yds/game to the WR2 role, above the ~36 norm.

Touchdown Board

Chase Brown is a bell-cow (68% of carries) meeting a defense that allows 0.49 RB rushing TDs/game — strong anytime-TD equity.

Mike Gesicki is a live anytime-TD dart — JAX are leaky to tight ends in the end zone (0.31 TE TDs/game vs ~0.24).

Brenton Strange is a live anytime-TD dart — CIN are leaky to tight ends in the end zone (0.47 TE TDs/game vs ~0.24).

In the red zone CIN throw it (64% pass inside the 20) — Ja'Marr Chase's TD equity over a goal-line back.

Game Script, Pace & Environment

Shootout profile — a 52 total between two non-run-first offenses points to volume passing on both sides; lean into the overs for the pass-catchers.

CIN — a pass-heavy offense

CIN stay aggressive through the air even with a lead — they pass 49% on early downs when ahead versus the league's 44%. They don't sit on the ball, which keeps their receivers live in scripts where most offenses would be running out the clock.

Chase Brown (13 carries, 58 yards) projects to his baseline workload — no strong script push either way in a close game.

Ja'Marr Chase projects for 9 targets and 83 yards, in line with his established role in a script that neither inflates nor suppresses the pass.

Underneath, Mike Gesicki (TE, 3 targets, 20 yards) is the dependable secondary read — and note the red zone stays TE-friendly regardless of score, so his touchdown equity holds up even if the game script shifts.

JAX — a balanced offense

JAX are a balanced offense — their run/pass split by game state tracks the league closely (43% pass when leading vs 44% average), so their players' usage is driven more by role than by any strong situational lean.

Chris Rodriguez Jr. (11 carries, 49 yards) projects to his baseline workload — no strong script push either way in a close game.

Parker Washington projects for 7 targets and 54 yards, in line with his established role in a script that neither inflates nor suppresses the pass.

Underneath, Brenton Strange (TE, 5 targets, 36 yards) is the dependable secondary read — and note the red zone stays TE-friendly regardless of score, so his touchdown equity holds up even if the game script shifts.

What to watch

The single biggest swing factor is availability — use the injury tool in the sidebar to mark anyone out; a starter's absence doesn't just remove his line, it redistributes his targets and carries to specific teammates, and the report and projections rebuild around it. Beyond that: if this game breaks toward the projected 2-point margin, the garbage-time backups (the ◆-flagged rows below) are where soft lines and real edge tend to appear — those depth players get fed in blowouts, and the market is slowest to price them.

This preview and the projections below regenerate through the week as injuries, weather and line moves update the inputs.
